title: Check yourself: Matching a tier to a workload

questions.stem: A team labels support tickets with one word each, and its tests show the cheapest tier is as accurate as the others. Which choice does the page back?

options.text: The newest release, since a later model has the lowest price
options.says: Ruled out because "A newer model can be cheaper than the one it replaces, and the reverse can happen".

options.text: The most capable tier, because ticket text can always hide a hard case
options.says: Ruled out because a tier above Opus is "earned by failing an evaluation, not assumed".

options.text: The middle tier, since it balances the tests against the price list
options.says: Ruled out because the method keeps "the cheapest tier that passes", not a tier in the middle.

options.text: The smallest model, since the extra capability above it buys nothing
options.says: The page's method is to move down "until quality drops, and keep the last tier that held", and the tests show nothing is lost at the cheapest tier.

questions.stem: A job feeds 300,000 tokens to a model and expects a short answer. One model is cheapest by price per million. What rules it out first?

options.text: Its context window is smaller than what is sent
options.says: The page says "a 300,000-token input rules Haiku 4.5 out whatever its price", because the input must fit the context window.

options.text: Its latency is the highest of all the models in the table
options.says: Ruled out because the latency column is relative and "depends on prompt length, output length, and thinking effort".

options.text: Its tokenizer is older than the tokenizers of the others
options.says: Ruled out because "A tokenizer change moves the count" and does not block an input.

options.text: Its output price is higher than its own input price
options.says: Ruled out because the page states "Output costs five times input on every row", which is a cost fact and not a limit.

questions.stem: A model lists a price 20% lower per token than its predecessor, but its tokenizer produces about 30% more tokens for the same text. What does the page's reasoning give for the cost of one task?

options.text: It stays equal, because a tokenizer change moves only the output side
options.says: Ruled out because "A tokenizer change moves the count."

options.text: It falls by about 20%, because the lower rate applies to the whole bill
options.says: Ruled out because the two facts "make the price per token a poor proxy for the price per task".

options.text: It rises by about 4%, because 0.8 x 1.3 is 1.04
options.says: The page says the newer tokenizer "produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text", so 0.8 times 1.3 is 1.04 times the cost per task.

options.text: It falls by about 10%, because the two changes average out
options.says: Ruled out because the page says to "compare cost per task on a sample, not per million tokens", and the two factors multiply rather than average.

origin.section: A price table is read, not guessed
